I've been farming this 7 mu in Quzhou for 40 years, and my university education taught me the science behind what my hands already knew from experience. My household has six people with some working off-farm, so I can't afford to waste labor on unnecessary operations, but I also know that skimping on inputs hurts my family's food security and income.

My winter wheat went in last October after rotary tillage — I planted an improved semi-dwarf variety at the right density. Now that spring has arrived and the wheat is greening up, I will topdress nitrogen at jointing based on tiller density. For the whole wheat season, I am targeting about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, split between basal and topdressing, plus about 8 kg of phosphorus and 6 kg of potassium from compound fertilizer. I will irrigate three times: at green-up if the soil is dry, again at jointing, and once more at grain filling. The well gives me reliable water, but pumping costs electricity, so I won't over-irrigate. For crop protection, I plan three sprays — herbicide for weeds, insecticide for aphids, and fungicide if powdery mildew appears, which it often does in our humid springs.

For summer maize, the window between wheat harvest in early June and maize sowing is brutally tight — usually less than a week. I will plant a hybrid maize variety using no-tillage directly into the wheat stubble to save time and preserve soil moisture. I will apply about 16 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, with a side-dress of urea at the V6 stage. I'll irrigate twice: once around tasseling and once at grain filling. Two pesticide applications should cover it — one pre-emergence herbicide and one insecticide if corn borer pressure builds. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize if the weather holds, which is what my land can reliably produce with good management.

My university background tells me that split nitrogen application and timely irrigation at jointing and filling are key to maximizing yield without wasting money, while 40 years of experience tells me not to over-complicate things on a small farm where family labor is limited. I use rotary tillage for wheat to establish a good seedbed in October, but no-tillage for maize in June because the turnaround is too short and soil moisture is too precious to disturb. I keep fertilizer rates moderate but sufficient — under-fertilizing risks a bad year that my family cannot afford, but over-fertilizing wastes cash on a 7 mu plot where every yuan matters.
